resources.name: attorneys
resources.title: Attorneys by county in Ohio, California, Michigan, Idaho, Arizona, Washington and Pennsylvania, from each bar's public counts
resources.description: How many lawyers each bar counts in each county, for seven states. Ohio: attorneys by county of address and status, from the Supreme Court of Ohio's attorney directory list (88 counties, with admission decade, private practice and Spanish speakers). California: active, inactive, judge and not-eligible licensees in each of the 58 counties, from the State Bar's county table. Michigan: active State Bar members living in each of the 83 counties, with private practice and the change from 2024. Idaho: members by status in each of the seven judicial districts. Arizona: active State Bar members in each of the 15 counties (the Bar's 2022 report). Washington: WSBA licensees of every type (lawyers plus limited licensees) in each of the 39 counties, with the attorney counts by member type. Pennsylvania: active attorneys in the seven counties the Disciplinary Board's annual report lists, and the Board's statewide status counts. Each record carries the source's own as-of date and a rate per 10,000 residents from the Census Bureau's county estimate. Only counts are published, and where a count is built from a directory file no name, birthdate, address or registration number is kept or written. In Ohio, counts in a disciplinary, deceased or other status, an admission decade, private practice or Spanish are published from five lawyers up, and only where no smaller count in the same group can be worked out from a county's total or the statewide figures. Every state record ties to its source's own total, and every published number is read a second time from the source file before release.

resources.name: federal-filings-county
resources.title: Federal civil cases filed, by county of the plaintiff's residence, case type and year (Federal Judicial Center)
resources.description: How many federal civil lawsuits are filed in each U.S. county, and of what kind, over the last ten complete federal fiscal years, from the Federal Judicial Center's Integrated Database (IDB). A case is counted in the county where the first-listed plaintiff lives (the first-listed defendant's county when the United States sues; the tract's county in land condemnation cases), by 16 nature-of-suit groups plus multidistrict litigations (MDLs), and rolled up to Probative's practice areas. One record per county carries all ten years, the prior-year change and the year-by-year history. Cases that cannot be placed in a county are published as rows of their own, per state and nationally: plaintiffs who live in the U.S. outside the court's state (with the MDL share), plaintiffs who live abroad, cases under a retired county code, and cases with an unrecorded county; district records add the same parts for each of the 94 district courts. Every state equals the sum of its counties and these rows, and the national total ties to the U.S. Courts' Table C-2 within a fraction of a percent. Only counts are published: no party, docket number or judge.

resources.name: firm-web-census
resources.title: US law firm websites: practices, Spanish, intake, by state, county and practice area
resources.description: US law firms, state by state and county by county, from two kinds of open source: law firms' own public websites, read at a slow, spaced rate each week (a few pages per firm), and official state registries published as open data for reuse (New York's attorney registrations and business entities, and the business registries of Colorado, Oregon, Connecticut, Texas and Pennsylvania). For each state, county and practice area we count the firms found, how many have a website we read, and, of those websites, the shares that show Spanish-language pages, a 24/7 intake statement, a free consultation or no fee unless they win, a chat or online booking tool, legal structured data (schema.org LegalService or Attorney), review markup or an llms.txt file, with the median number of pages a firm has about the practice. Every row gives two coverage measures: the firms found against the employer law offices the Census Bureau's County Business Patterns counts, and the websites read against our estimate of the law firms with a website. A state is called a census only when the first reaches 0.70; until then the rows are a sample. These counts are CC BY 4.0. The firm-level rows behind them (name as the firm or registry gives it, offices by county and the yes-or-no facts, each linked to the page it was read on with the date) are published separately under the Open Database License (ODbL) 1.0, because the list of sites comes partly from OpenStreetMap (© OpenStreetMap contributors), and are shown on the /firms/ pages. No firm is rated, scored or ranked. Firm names can include a lawyer's name when that is the firm's registered or website name; a row that is only one person's name is counted and not listed. Website sources: Common Crawl (its web graph and the Web Data Commons structured-data extract), OpenStreetMap and Wikidata.

resources.name: state-courts

resources.description: How many cases are filed in state trial courts, by county, court level and case group, from each state court system's own published statistics. Texas (Office of Court Administration): district, constitutional county and statutory county courts, fiscal years 2023–24 and 2024–25, with district-court filings by case type. Washington (Administrative Office of the Courts): superior courts and district and municipal courts (criminal, civil, domestic, probate, juvenile, traffic, DUI, protection orders, small claims), calendar year 2025. Maryland (Judiciary data dashboard): circuit-court filings by case type and District Court filings (landlord-tenant, civil, criminal, DUI, traffic citations, peace orders), fiscal years 2012 to 2025. Indiana (Office of Judicial Administration): circuit and superior court new filings by Rule 8 case type (felony, misdemeanor, tort, collection, small claims, eviction, foreclosure, domestic relations, estates, juvenile), calendar year 2025 (provisional) beside 2024. Wisconsin (Director of State Courts Office): circuit-court cases opened by category, felony to juvenile, 2020 to 2025. Virginia (Office of the Executive Secretary): circuit, general district and juvenile and domestic relations district courts by locality (county or independent city), calendar year 2025. Pennsylvania (Administrative Office of Pennsylvania Courts): courts of common pleas in all 67 counties, civil cases by type (motor-vehicle and other torts, mass torts, malpractice, contract and debt, landlord-tenant, foreclosure) and criminal, protection from abuse, support, custody, divorce, juvenile, adoption and guardianship cases, calendar year 2024. Oregon (Oregon Judicial Department): circuit courts in all 36 counties, calendar year 2025. West Virginia (Supreme Court of Appeals): circuit, family and magistrate courts in all 55 counties, calendar year 2025. Nebraska (Judicial Branch): county and district courts in all 93 counties and the separate juvenile courts of three of them, fiscal year 2024–25. Maine (Judicial Branch): superior courts, unified criminal dockets and district courts in all 16 counties, fiscal years 2021–22 to 2025–26. California (Judicial Council): superior courts in all 58 counties (motor-vehicle and other injury, limited civil, eviction, small claims, felony, misdemeanor, traffic, marital, parentage, domestic violence, child support, juvenile delinquency and dependency, guardianship, other probate, mental health), fiscal year 2024–25. Louisiana (Supreme Court of Louisiana, Judicial Administrator's Office): district courts in 61 of the state's 64 parishes (civil, criminal, traffic and juvenile cases), calendar year 2025 beside 2024 where the 2024 report's row matches. Hawaii (Hawaii State Judiciary): circuit courts in all four circuits, each mapped to its county (motor-vehicle and other injury, contract, foreclosure, probate proceedings, circuit criminal cases), fiscal year 2024–25. Every record keeps the state's own category names and the numbers added into each group (components), and carries a harmonized group and the practice areas it bears on, so a county's filings can be read as demand for personal injury, family, landlord-tenant, small claims and debt, probate, criminal and DUI, juvenile and traffic work. In every source the counties add up to the state's own printed total where it prints one (Texas, Washington, Indiana, Wisconsin, Virginia, Pennsylvania, Oregon, West Virginia, Nebraska, Hawaii), Louisiana's parish records are the parishes whose rows add up to the printed district totals and its state row is the state's printed total, and the state rows for Maryland are the sum of the counties.
